hook: Meaning, as **math**. Five concepts and you'll understand the technology half of Stage 4.

scenes.title: Meaning → a **list of numbers**
scenes.sub: A point in space where distance = difference in meaning
scenes.narration: An embedding is a vector — a list of numbers — that a model produces to represent the MEANING of a piece of text. 'Cat chases mouse' becomes something like five hundred floating-point numbers. The magic is geometric: texts with similar meanings get vectors that point in similar directions. Meaning has become measurable — not by reading, but by measuring angles between lists of numbers. Every search bar, recommendation, and RAG system in this course stands on this one idea.

Watch it happen. The phrase 'quarterly report' goes into the embedding model, and out comes a point in space — one number per dimension, 1,536 of them for a typical OpenAI model. No single number means anything readable; meaning lives in the PATTERN across all of them. Change a word — 'annual report' — and the point moves slightly. Change the topic entirely — 'chocolate cake' — and it moves far. Similar direction, similar meaning. That's the entire trick.

scenes.title: 384, 768, 1,536 — how many **numbers** do you need?
scenes.sub: Bigger = richer meaning, heavier storage and compute
scenes.narration: Embedding models differ in dimension count — small models produce 384 or 768 numbers; flagship models, one thousand five hundred thirty-six or more. Trade-offs: higher dimensions capture finer semantic distinctions — 'bank' the river versus 'bank' the finance institution separate more cleanly — but every vector costs storage, memory, and compute forever. A million documents at 1,536 dimensions is 6 gigabytes of raw floats before any index overhead. Pick the smallest dimensionality that passes YOUR eval — this is a workload decision, not a prestige one.

items.s: Raw vectors alone — an HNSW index typically adds 20-50% on top
Same corpus, 4x lighter — if quality holds on your eval, it's the right call

items.t: Dimensions are locked to the model
items.s: Changing models = re-embedding everything (GA-08 covers the migration)

scenes.narration: The arithmetic to keep in your pocket. Memory footprint is documents times dimensions times bytes per float — float32 at four bytes; some stores support float16 or quantization to halve that. The index adds its own overhead. And remember: dimensions are a property of the MODEL, not the data — you can't downsize retroactively without re-embedding. This is why the model choice in the next reel has long-tail consequences: you're committing to a geometry for your whole corpus.

scenes.title: Cosine, dot, Euclidean — **which ruler?**
scenes.sub: Usually cosine. The others matter in specific setups.
scenes.narration: Three rulers for comparing vectors, and you met the math in Reel 16. Cosine similarity — angle only, ignoring length — the default for text embeddings because direction encodes meaning. Dot product — angle times length; equals cosine when vectors are normalized, and it's the cheapest to compute. Euclidean distance — straight-line distance — sensible when magnitudes carry information, common in some image and recommendation setups. Your vector store will ask which one; for text embeddings, the answer is cosine unless your model's documentation says otherwise.

items.s: Text default — 'bank' river vs finance separates via angle, not size
If you normalize at write time, dot product IS cosine — free speed
Some image/recsys models train magnitudes to mean confidence

scenes.narration: Choosing rules. Text embeddings: cosine, or dot with pre-normalized vectors — normalize once at ingestion and the cheaper dot product gives identical rankings. Some embedding models — notably certain image and recommendation models — bake information into vector length, making Euclidean appropriate. The action item: check your model's documentation for its intended metric, and normalize upfront if you want dot-product speed with cosine semantics. One less thing to think about at query time.

scenes.title: 'sofa' ≠ 'couch' — **unless you search by meaning**
scenes.sub: Keyword finds matches. Semantic finds meaning. You need both.
scenes.narration: Keyword search — like SQL LIKE or BM25 — matches literal tokens. Search 'sofa' and documents saying 'couch' are invisible. Semantic search finds by meaning: 'couch' and 'sofa' sit close in embedding space, so both surface. But semantic has its own blind spots: exact codes, error strings, product numbers, and people's names — things where the literal string IS the meaning. SKU 'AX-2041' must match 'AX-2041', not something semantically adjacent. This is why mature systems use hybrid search — both signals fused — a reel we'll build to in GA-15.

cards.s: Exact tokens, fast, interpretable. Misses synonyms; brittle to typos and phrasing.
Matches meaning across synonyms and phrasing. Blurry on exact codes; can drift.

scenes.narration: Side by side. Keyword: the classic inverted index — precise, explainable, but deaf to synonyms and word order nuance. Semantic: meaning-space retrieval — forgiving of phrasing, powerful for concepts, but it can rank a 'similar enough' wrong answer above an exact match, and it hallucinates neighbors for rare tokens like serial numbers. Neither wins alone; the systems you'll build fuse them. Hold this comparison — GA-15 turns it into a retrieval architecture.

scenes.title: 1,536 dimensions → a **picture**
scenes.sub: PCA & t-SNE: projection, lossy but honest
scenes.narration: You can't see 1,536 dimensions — nobody can. But you can PROJECT them down to two or three for visualization, and the patterns survive. PCA — the linear workhorse — finds the directions of maximum variance and flattens along them; fast, stable, great for a first look. t-SNE — the famous one — bends space nonlinearly so neighbors stay neighbors; gorgeous clusters, but distances between clusters can mislead. Use projections to sanity-check your embeddings: do invoices cluster apart from contracts? Do Hindi and English versions of the same policy sit together? Meaning you can SEE is meaning you can debug.

A flattened view of a healthy corpus. Invoices cluster with invoices — orange together. Contracts form their own island — teal. And look at the green pair: the English policy and its Hindi translation sit close — cross-lingual meaning survived the projection. When your real corpus plots like THIS, retrieval will work. When it plots as mush — everything overlapping randomly — the problem is upstream: bad chunking, a mismatched embedding model, or documents that aren't actually what you think they are.

scenes.title: Concepts done — now pick your model
scenes.next: Reel 23 · Embedding Models — choosing, batching, and the re-embedding bill

recap: Embeddings = meaning as vectors; similar direction = similar meaning
Dimensions trade quality for memory; cosine is the default metric (dot if normalized)
Semantic search finds meaning, keyword finds literals — visualize with PCA/t-SNE to debug your corpus

quiz.q: Why does keyword search fail on the query 'sofa' when the document says 'couch'?
opts: Keyword search matches literal tokens — it has no notion of synonymy
Both words have too many letters
quiz.why: BM25-style search matches tokens, not meanings. 'Sofa' and 'couch' share no tokens — semantic search closes that gap.

quiz.q: When does dot product equal cosine similarity?
opts: When both vectors are normalized to unit length
quiz.why: cos = dot/(‖a‖·‖b‖); with unit norms the denominator is 1 — so normalize once at ingestion and use the cheaper dot product.

quiz.q: Your projected embedding plot shows everything as one undifferentiated blob. Most likely cause?
opts: Upstream problems: bad chunking, wrong embedding model for the content, or mislabeled documents
quiz.why: Healthy corpora cluster by topic in projection. A blob signals the embeddings aren't capturing meaningful structure — debug chunking and model fit first.

code.title: Embeddings, from text to plot
code.body:
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

client = OpenAI()

def embed(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    r = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=texts)
    return np.array([d.embedding for d in r.data])

docs = [
    "Quarterly revenue rose 12% to $4.1M",
    "Q1 earnings: total income $4.1 million, up 12%",
    "The sofa arrives in grey fabric on Friday",
    "Error AX-2041: printer queue timeout",
    "Policy updated: remote work now 3 days per week",
    "नई नीति: दूरस्थ कार्य अब सप्ताह में 3 दिन",
]
vecs = embed(docs)                     # (6, 1536)
print(vecs.shape)

# similarity sanity check (unit-normalized → dot = cosine)
u = vecs / np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
sim = u @ u.T
print("revenue pair:", round(sim[0, 1], 3))   # high — paraphrase
print("revenue vs sofa:", round(sim[0, 2], 3)) # near 0 — unrelated

# 1536 → 2 for a look
xy = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(vecs)
plt.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1])
for (x, y), d in zip(xy, docs):
    plt.annotate(d[:20], (x, y))
plt.show()                              # clusters = healthy corpus
annot: text-embedding-3-small: 1536 dims, cheap, strong — the default workhorse
Paraphrase pairs should score > 0.8; unrelated < 0.2 — calibrate on known pairs
PCA plot: same-topic docs should hug; cross-lingual pairs should neighbor

notes:
# Embedding Concepts

## What is an embedding
- Text → fixed-length vector of floats; **similar direction = similar meaning**.
- Meaning becomes measurable geometry.

## Dimensions
- 384 / 768 / 1536 / 3072… richer ≠ always better.
- Memory: 1M docs × 1536 × 4B ≈ 6 GB (+index). Pick the smallest size that passes your eval.
- Dimensions are model-locked → model change = full re-embedding (GA-08).

## Similarity metrics
| Metric | When |
| --- | --- |
| **Cosine** | text default (direction only) |
| Dot | normalized vectors → == cosine, faster |
| Euclidean | when magnitude carries signal (some image/recsys) |
- Normalize at write time → query with cheap dot product.

## Semantic vs keyword
- Keyword: exact tokens — precise on codes/IDs, deaf to synonyms.
- Semantic: meaning — synonym-robust, blurry on exact strings.
- Production answer: **hybrid** (GA-15).

## Visualizing
- PCA: fast linear projection — first look.
- t-SNE: cluster-preserving, nonlinear — pretty, distorts global distances.
- Healthy corpus → topic clusters + cross-lingual neighbors. Blob → fix chunking/model upstream.
